examples: The temperature is really high today.
At night the temperature is much lower.
It is cold because the temperature dropped.
nuance: Gi-on means the air temperature as a number and pairs with 높다 high or 낮다 low, while 날씨 is the broader feel of the weather.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 온도 for objects.

examples: I watch the weather forecast in the morning.
The forecast was right so I brought an umbrella.
The forecast said it will rain.
nuance: Il-gi-ye-bo means the weather forecast you see on the news, and Koreans often check it daily and say 일기예보를 보다 to watch it.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 날씨 for weather itself.

examples: The rainy season started in summer.
The rainy season is long so it rains every day.
An umbrella is essential during the rainy season.
nuance: Jang-ma is the long summer rainy season in Korea around July, a humid period of steady rain that is very different from a single rainy day.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 비 for ordinary rain.

examples: They say a typhoon is coming tomorrow.
Because a typhoon came I cannot go outside.
The typhoon passed and the weather cleared up.
nuance: Tae-pung means a typhoon and uses the verb 오다 to come like rain and snow, and these storms hit Korea mostly in late summer.
mistakes: Do not say 태풍이 불어요 like wind.

examples: The rain stopped and a rainbow appeared.
The rainbow in the sky is really pretty.
Today I saw a rainbow for the first time.
nuance: Mu-ji-gae means a rainbow and appears with the verb 뜨다 to rise, so 무지개가 뜨다 is the natural way to say a rainbow appears.
mistakes: Do not say 무지개가 와요 like rain.

examples: It got very foggy in the morning.
The fog is thick so I cannot see ahead.
The fog cleared and the sun came out.
nuance: An-gae means fog and uses the verb 끼다 to settle like clouds, so 안개가 끼다 is the standard way to say it becomes foggy.
mistakes: Do not say 안개가 와요 like rain.

examples: The sunlight is really strong today.
The sunlight is warm so I feel good.
Sunlight comes in through the window.
nuance: Haet-bit means sunlight, the visible light from the sun, and pairs with 강하다 strong or 따뜻하다 warm to describe how it feels on a clear day.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 햇살 in nuance.

examples: It was hot so I rested in the shade.
The tree shade is really cool.
I went to the shade and drank water.
nuance: Geu-neul means shade, the cool dark area away from sunlight, and is the natural opposite of 햇빛, often a welcome spot on a hot day.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 그림자 for a cast shadow.

examples: This summer the heat is really severe.
I am very sensitive to heat.
I could not sleep because of the heat.
nuance: Deo-wi means the heat as a feeling and pairs with 타다 in 더위를 타다 to mean you suffer in hot weather, while 추위 is its opposite.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 덥다 the adjective.

examples: This winter the cold is really severe.
I am very sensitive to cold.
I wore many clothes because of the cold.
nuance: Chu-wi means the cold as a feeling and pairs with 타다 in 추위를 타다 to mean you suffer in cold weather, while 더위 is its opposite.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 춥다 the adjective.

examples: I am really happy because the first snow came.
I want to see the first snow together.
nuance: Cheon-nun means the first snow of the season and carries a romantic feeling in Korea, where seeing it with someone is treated as a special moment.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 눈 for ordinary snow.

examples: It rained so I wore rain boots.
The child likes yellow rain boots.
Rain boots are needed during the rainy season.
nuance: Jang-hwa means rubber rain boots worn on wet days and takes the verb 신다 to wear like all footwear, often paired with rainy weather.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 신발 for ordinary shoes.
